## Overview

The Eora are an Aboriginal Australian people of the coastal area of what is now the Sydney basin in New South Wales. Their territory included sandstone coastal outcrops and ridges, coves, mangrove swamps, creeks and tidal lagoons. It extended from the northern shores of Port Jackson towards the Hawkesbury River plateau, around Pittwater, south to Botany Bay and the Georges River, and west to Parramatta. The Eora spoke a coastal variety of the Sydney language, related to the inland variety known as Dharug or Darug, within the Yuin–Kuric group. The term Eora was recorded by First Fleet officers, usually translated as “men” or “people,” and was later adopted as an ethnonym. Their population was severely reduced after colonisation through smallpox, other introduced diseases, starvation and the destruction of food resources. Descendants live on, although much of the earlier language, social system and way of life has been lost.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Eora textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

They do record a colonial encounter in which a sailor dropped his pants, clarifying to the Eora that the visitors were not ghosts and revealing the misunderstanding surrounding the newcomers’ sex. The sources also mention scarring on women’s temples, which Governor Phillip incorrectly interpreted as evidence of mistreatment of women; the marks were traces of mourning practices. This is the only bodily appearance or dress-related practice described in the supplied material.

### Architecture

Eora people made extensive use of rock shelters. Many of these shelters were later destroyed by settlers who mined their rich concentrations of phosphates for manure. During the early colonial period, Governor Phillip built a brick house for Bennelong at Tubowgulle, the site now associated with Bennelong Point and the Sydney Opera House; the hut was demolished five years later. This building was a colonial construction rather than a documented Eora architectural form.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They do describe bark canoes, used for close-to-shore navigation, fishing, cooking and eating in bays and harbours. Eora people used nets for catching mullet, lines for fish, burley and spears from rock ledges, and rock shelters as places connected with subsistence. The language sources preserve words for tools and objects associated with Aboriginal languages, including *wamarang* and *bumarit*, combined in the English word boomerang, and *wamara*, associated with the English word woomera.

## Jewelry & body adornment

They do mention scarring on women’s temples as a mourning practice. No materials, techniques, ritual sequence or adornment terminology beyond this observation are given.

## Music & performance

One Eora song has survived in written musical form. Bennelong and Yemmerrawanne sang it at a concert in London in 1793. Edward Jones, identified as Bardd y Brenin, transcribed its words and music, and the material was published in 1811. A modern version was performed by Clarence Slockee and Matthew Doyle at the State Library of NSW in August 2010 and was made available online.

The sources also describe later public uses of reconstructed or revived language in performance. In December 2020, Olivia Fox sang a version of Australia’s national anthem in Eora or Dharug at a Tri Nations Test match between Australia and Argentina. The reconstructed language has also been used in welcome ceremonies conducted by Dharug people. The supplied material does not name Eora musical instruments, song genres, instrumental ensembles, dance accompaniment, musical scales or performance rules.

## Dance & theatre

They mention *corroboree* as an English word derived from a Darug or possibly Tharawal-language form, *garabara*. The material does not provide a description of the performance, its choreography, its social setting or its relationship to Eora ceremonial life.

## Festivals & rituals

They do provide information about mourning, conflict and several colonial-era social practices. Scarring on women’s temples was connected with mourning. Formal battles used to settle inter-clan grievances were limited in time: they began late in the afternoon and ceased shortly after twilight.

Eora subsistence followed seasonal patterns. Summer foods included oysters, netted mullet, fish caught on a line, and larger fish taken with burley and speared from rock ledges. As summer ended, turtle feasting was described as a prized occasion. Winter activities included foraging for and hunting possum, echidna, fruit bats, wallaby and kangaroo. These seasonal food practices are the only recurring calendar-related traditions described in the supplied sources.

The colonial period also introduced imposed institutional practices. Governor Macquarie established a Native Institution for Aboriginal and Māori children, with parents permitted to visit only on 28 December each year. The sources describe the institution as disastrous, with many children dying there.

## Foodways

Eora people were largely coastal dwellers and lived mainly from the produce of the sea. They were described as expert in fishing, cooking and eating in the bays and harbours, using bark canoes for close-to-shore navigation and food gathering. They did not grow or plant crops. Women picked herbs used in herbal remedies.

Wetland management was important, and the Queenscliff, Curl Curl and Dee Why lagoons furnished abundant food that was collected seasonally. Summer foods included oysters and mullet caught in nets. Fat fish were caught on a line, while larger fish were taken with burley and speared from rock ledges. Turtle was associated with a prized feast as summer ended. Winter foods included possum, echidna, fruit bats, wallaby and kangaroo. They do state that Bennelong learned about British food needs, etiquette, weaponry and hierarchy during his period of captivity and association with the colony.

## Oral tradition & literature

One Eora song has survived through the performance of Bennelong and Yemmerrawanne in London in 1793, its transcription by Edward Jones, and its publication in 1811.

Language documentation is central to the recorded preservation effort. William Dawes recorded the traditional tongue of the elder people of Sydney from Patyegarang, and his notebooks became a major source for later reconstruction. Other wordlists and notebooks were compiled by First Fleeters and later contributors, including David Collins, John Hunter, Philip Gidley King, Daniel Southwell, Watkin Tench, David Blackburn, Henry Fulton, Daniel Paine and James Bowman.

From the 1990s and 2000s, descendants of Dharug clans in Western Sydney made considerable efforts to revive the language. A 2005 master’s thesis by Jeremy Steele analysed its grammar, and a reconstructed form has been used in speeches, school demonstrations and welcome ceremonies. Some children at Chifley College’s Dunheved campus had begun learning it by 2005.

## Language & religion

The Eora spoke the coastal variety of the Sydney language, also referred to as Iyora, Iora or Eora. The language belongs to the Yuin–Kuric group. The inland variety has been called Dharug, Darug or Dharuk, while the coastal variety has been distinguished from the hinterland form. The sources state that the speakers did not use a specific name for their language before settlement by the First Fleet, and that neither Dharug nor Eora appears in the historical record as a language name in the relevant account.

The language became extinct in everyday use through colonisation, social upheaval and increasing use of English and New South Wales Pidgin, although reconstructed forms are now being taught and performed. They do record mourning practices, seasonal food observances and relationships with country, waterways and food-gathering places.
